right_to_work_note: Alabama law says no worker can be forced to join a union or pay union dues to keep a job.
public_bargaining_note: Alabama has no statewide bargaining law for public workers, but firefighters have a meet-and-confer law and some cities bargain with their workers voluntarily.
public_strike_note: Alabama courts have ruled that strikes by public employees are illegal.
state_note: Alabama's right-to-work protection is written into the state constitution, added by voters in 2016.

right_to_work_note: Alaska has no right-to-work law, so a union contract may require workers to pay dues or fees for representation.
public_bargaining_note: State law gives most public employees, including teachers and state workers, the right to bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions.
public_strike_note: Most public employees may strike only after mediation and a majority vote, and police, firefighters, prison guards, and hospital workers may not strike at all.
state_note: Alaska is one of the few states where public employees can legally strike, but only after mediation and a majority vote, and workers who protect public health and safety cannot strike at all.

right_to_work_note: Right-to-work is in Arizona's constitution, so no worker can be forced to join a union or pay dues to keep a job.
public_bargaining_note: Arizona has no statewide bargaining law; public safety workers may join a union, state executive-branch workers have a meet-and-confer policy, and some cities bargain under local rules.
public_strike_note: Arizona's attorney general and courts have said public employees do not have the right to strike.
state_note: Arizona was one of the first states to adopt right-to-work, writing it into the state constitution in 1946.

right_to_work_note: Arkansas's constitution says no worker can be forced to join a union or pay dues to keep a job.
public_bargaining_note: Arkansas has no statewide law giving public employees the right to bargain collectively.
public_strike_note: Arkansas courts have ruled that public employees have no right to strike against the government.
agency_name: Arkansas Department of Labor and Licensing
state_note: In 2023 Arkansas banned public employers from deducting union dues from workers' paychecks.

right_to_work_note: California has no right-to-work law, so a union contract may require workers to pay dues or fees for representation.
public_bargaining_note: State law gives most state and local public employees the right to bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions.
public_strike_note: California courts have said public employees may strike, but only after mediation and fact-finding are finished.
state_note: California is one of the few states where courts have said public employees may strike, but only after the full dispute process is finished.

right_to_work_note: Colorado has no right-to-work law, but its Labor Peace Act says a union can require dues only if 75% of the workers vote for it.
public_bargaining_note: State employees can bargain since 2020 and county employees since 2022, but most city, school, and special-district workers have no bargaining law.
public_strike_note: Colorado's supreme court recognized a limited right to strike for some public workers, but the county bargaining law bars a union from ordering a strike.
agency_name: Colorado Department of Labor and Employment
state_note: Colorado's Labor Peace Act is one of a kind: a union can require dues only if 75% of workers vote for it.

right_to_work_note: Connecticut has no right-to-work law, so a union contract may require workers to pay dues or fees for representation.
public_bargaining_note: State law gives state, city, and public school employees the right to bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions.
public_strike_note: Connecticut law bans strikes by public employees, and courts can order workers back to work.
agency_name: Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations
state_note: Connecticut bans public-sector strikes, and its labor board hears complaints and can enforce the ban in court.

right_to_work_note: Delaware has no right-to-work law, so a union contract may require workers to pay dues or fees for representation.
public_bargaining_note: State law gives public employees, including public school teachers, the right to bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions.
public_strike_note: Delaware law bans strikes by public employees.
state_note: Delaware public employees can bargain collectively, but public-sector strikes are illegal.

right_to_work_note: Right-to-work is in Florida's constitution, so no worker can be forced to join a union or pay dues to keep a job.
public_bargaining_note: Florida's constitution guarantees public employees the right to bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions.
public_strike_note: Florida's constitution guarantees bargaining but expressly bans strikes by public employees.
state_note: A 2023 Florida law requires public-sector unions to keep at least 60% of workers as dues-paying members or risk losing their certification, and it ended most public-employer dues deductions.

right_to_work_note: Georgia law says no worker can be forced to join a union or pay dues to keep a job.
public_bargaining_note: Georgia law bans collective bargaining for public employees, except firefighters, and teachers are specifically barred from bargaining.
public_strike_note: Public employee strikes are illegal in Georgia.
state_note: Georgia is one of the few states that bans public-sector collective bargaining outright — only firefighters are allowed to bargain.
